ESKOM GHOST VILLAGE

By: Latashia Naidoo | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
A story of how Eskom has wasted hundreds of millions of rand on a "ghost" development, while at the same time seeking to raise power prices for South Africans.

Summary:
More than a decade after it was conceived as a solution for worker accommodation at Eskom’s Kusile Power Station, the Wilge Residential Village remains exactly what it has quietly become: a taxpayer-funded ghost town.
Built to house hundreds of construction staff during Kusile’s build, the 336-unit complex has never meaningfully housed anyone.
Instead, it has swallowed close to R1-billion, ballooning from an original budget of around R160 million. That works out to roughly R2.5 million per empty apartment.

Investigations dating back to the News24 Eskom Files in 2021 exposed how procurement inside the project spiralled into excess, including inflated furniture tenders and alleged collusion between officials and contractors.
Items like desks, couches and even leisure equipment were reportedly marked up far beyond market value. The spending kept flowing. Occupants never came.

Fast forward to 2025 and now early 2026, and nothing fundamental has changed:
• The buildings stand unfinished and unoccupied
• The site shows visible decay and vandalism
• Attempts to sell or transfer the property have not materialised
• Parliament and opposition MPs continue to label it fruitless and wasteful expenditure
• The Special Investigating Unit has kept Wilge within broader Eskom corruption probes, but no public recovery of funds or prosecutions linked specifically to the village have been announced.
All the while, Eskom has paid for alternative accommodation and transport for workers the village was meant to house, effectively paying twice.

The optics are stark. N almost-billion-plus housing estate sitting empty in a province battling housing backlogs and unemployment, while the utility asks consumers for tariff hikes.
But Wilge is not just an abandoned development. It is a physical monument to state capture era procurement, weak oversight and consequence-free spending.
A concrete reminder that billions were lost not only in coal contracts and power station delays, but also in the small, supposedly practical things. Housing. Beds. Roofs.


As of 2026, Wilge is still empty. Still decaying. Still paid for. And there’s still no accountability.

ESKOM GHOST VILLAGE - FINAL:

(LOURENSA): At first glance, it looks exactly as it should.

(LOURENSA): A housing development on the outskirts of eMalahleni in Mpumalanga, about 100km east of Johannesburg.

(LOURENSA): Rows of apartment blocks, finished facades; even a water treatment facility.

(LOURENSA): This is Eskom’s Wilge Residential Village.

(LOURENSA: Nine apartment blocks. 336 units.

(LOURENSA): Built with public money. Close to a billion rand…

(LOURENSA): … for a place that was never lived in.

(FTB)

(LOURENSA LINK): This is Kusile - Eskom’s flagship new coal power station. It’s one of the largest infrastructure projects ever undertaken in South Africa. Now a project of that scale requires housing for the workers building the power station - which is where our story begins.

(LOURENSA): Kusile Power Station sits on the coalfields of Mpumalanga, about 16 kilometres from eMalahleni. In the early 2010s, construction was at its peak. Thousands of artisans, engineers, and labourers were moving through the site.

(LOURENSA): Eskom needed to house them. The plan: a dedicated residential development nearby for workers at all stages of the Kusile build.

(LOURENSA): The project was conceived in 2010, went out to tender in October 2011, and by July 2012, the contract was awarded to the Liviero Group - one of South Africa’s largest construction companies at the time.

(LOURENSA LINK): When Eskom approved the project in 2012, the price tag was R160 million.

(LOURENSA): On paper, it was a straightforward build. A tight budget. A clear deadline. And a project already underway.
(LOURENSA): But behind the paperwork, there were early signs that something wasn’t right.
(LOURENSA): One senior site official agreed to speak to us, as long as we hid his identity. We're calling him David.

(DAVID SUBTITLES): “I started as a senior safety officer. The site was in a very bad condition - rubble all over the place. You couldn’t even walk between the partially-built buildings, half-built scaffolds. Eskom stopped the site because of safety reasons, so I was thrown into the deep end there. But we made it work and turned the site around.”

(LOURENSA): But that momentum didn’t last.

(DAVID SUBTITLES): “There were labour-related issues that started coming through - strikes, disruptions - and that definitely had an impact… on how work was scheduled and slowed things down in certain areas.”

(LOURENSA): And the cause, according to those closest to it, came down to money.

(DAVID SUBTITLES): “When payments become a problem, work can’t continue. It reaches a point where things just stop - and that’s what happened here.”

(LOURENSA): For the workers on the ground, like scaffolder Percy Mtshweni, the consequences were abrupt.

(PERCY MTSHWENI): “One day we just woke up… got ready, went to work. When we got there, it was locked. There was just security personnel there. They told us that the company that we were employed to came, sent some trucks during the night. All the equipment that they had there, they took all of it.”

(LOURENSA): Overnight - it was over.

(LOURENSA): In April 2014, weeks after the initial deadline, Liviero formally walked off site.

(LOURENSA): At the centre of the dispute - a project labour agreement. A deal between Eskom and unions to set wages, conditions, and who gets hired on site.

(KEVIN MILEHAM): “Eskom had been negotiating with the labour unions and they had said they wanted this project labour agreement enforced. But that added costs. The contractor then came back and said well it’s going to cost you more. And Eskom said, okay, we’ll pay. And they paid for a couple of months, and then they stopped paying the extra.”

(LOURENSA): Kevin Mileham, the DA’s spokesperson for electricity and energy, shows us around.

(LOURENSA): "I'm going to try to get inside. But you’ve been here before?"

(KEVIN MILEHAM): "I have, yeah, a few times. Every time it's a little bit more dilapidated, a little bit more run down."

(LOURENSA): "Is there any work done…’

(KEVIN MILEHAM): “No…”

(LOURENSA): ‘…to keep the building in good shape?"

(KEVIN MILEHAM): "No. They do the bare minimum to ensure that it's secure. And they leave it at that."

(LOURENSA): Inside, the apartments are startlingly close to finished. In fact, construction stopped when the development was 98% complete.

(KEVIN MILEHAM): "You forward to 2014 and the contractor says: we're not getting the money that we're supposed to get for this. So they walk off site - and then starts a whole lot of disputes, court cases, etcetra.”

(LOURENSA): By 2018, Liviero was in financial distress and entered business rescue. In December 2019, construction was formally halted.

(LOURENSA LINK): By the time development had stalled in 2018, it had ballooned to nearly R1 billion.
And that’s public money… for buildings that today stand empty.

(LOURENSA): From R160 million to nearly R1 billion. And yet - Eskom kept spending.
(LOURENSA): Desks and couches - marked up nearly 800 percent from retail.
(LOURENSA): And a total R22 million on furnishings. Bought… after construction had already stopped.
(LOURENSA): Unoccupied and unguarded, the site became a target.

PERCY MTSHWENI): “For people, it was like (inviting criminals from outside. People were now seeing an opportunity there - to go there and take the stuff that was there, the windows and the... There was a lot of things that were happening there.”

(LOURENSA): The damage ran deeper than theft for the community.

(ELIJAH MASHIANE): “To say there has been a meeting that was held with the community, from one of the members or executives from Eskom, to actually explain to the community as to what actually happened to the buildings, there hasn’t - it was never.”
(LOURENSA): ‘Even to today?’
(ELIJAH MASHIANE): “Even til today.”

(LOURENSA): Elijah Mashiane had staked his career on Wilge.

(LOURENSA): ‘You sort of planned your future around the development - in studying to become a millwright.’
(ELIJAH MASHIANE): “Yes. You know, I actually had high hopes - employment, you know, everything, you know. And having to see what actually happened to those buildings… what I’ve actually planned for myself now - I have to now, you know, choose a different stream.”

(PAUSE)

(LOURENSA): While the Wilge Complex stood empty, Eskom had to make a different plan to house the workers.

(DAVID SUBTITLES): “What didn’t make sense from a site perspective was that you had this development here. And at the same time people were being accommodated elsewhere. That was difficult to understand.”

(LOURENSA): Eskom appointed 46 companies to accommodate contractors in surrounding towns - at a cost of around R1.2 billion.

(LOURENSA): One company received the lion’s share of that budget.

(LOURENSA): Quatra M Investments, based in eMalahleni, was paid around R894 million. Its role: leasing, managing, and supplying accommodation facilities for Kusile contractors.

(LOURENSA): Then we found a connection.

(LOURENSA): Abram Masango - Eskom’s former head of capital projects - oversaw Kusile during the years of delays and cost overruns. He’s now under investigation over procurement tied to the project.

(LOURENSA): Company records show a link.

LOURENSA: So we went to find out more.

(LOURENSA): “Hello. Is there anyone we can talk to about the Kusile accommodation contracts?”
(EMPLOYEE SUBTITLES): “I spoke to the director, he says he has responded on email.”
(LOURENSA): ‘Ya, we did get an email response.’
(EMPLOYEE SUBTITLES): “We did respond on that. There is a court case between ourselves and Eskom unfortunately.”
(LOURENSA): “We understand that. But this is a matter of public interest. And we wanted to give you an opportunity to respond on camera.”
(EMPLOYEE SUBTITLES): “Unfortunately I can’t phone him again. I’m sure the lawyers will be able to probably provide.”

(LOURENSA): Quatra M declined to speak on camera. In writing, one of the directors denied any involvement in Wilge and any improper links to Masango, calling the Wilge project ‘a total disaster that should never have been built.’

(LOURENSA): In court, the two parties are disputing those Kusile contracts and the money tied to them.

(LOURENSA): And those who were there say it didn’t happen by accident.

(DAVID SUBTITLES): “It was a lot of stuff. It was a lot of politicians I know that came to the site - I’m not gonna say names. It was also in the timeframe that Brian Molefe was running Eskom. I don’t know what went on there - well we all know what went on there - Eskom never paid us.”

(FTB)

(LOURENSA): To date, not a cent has been recovered.
In writing, Eskom confirmed the full project cost of R939 million.

(LOURENSA): In 2019, Eskom instituted disciplinary action against the manager responsible. The process concluded in January 2020 with that manager’s dismissal.

(LOURENSA): ‘Is this part of the whole corruption cloud hanging over Kusile, and procurement regarding the build of the power station, or should we view this as a separate matter?’

(KEVIN MILEHAM): ‘I think it’s indicative of a much broader systemic problem at Eskom, particularly over the state capture period. But we’re in a situation now where there’s still no accountability, where people still aren’t facing the consequences of their actions.’

(LOURENSA): The independent public integrity and anti-corruption authority, The Special Investigating Unit is probing the project. No criminal charges have been laid.

(LOURENSA): For David, Wilge’s failure lies solely with Eskom.

(DAVID SUBTITLES): “About two years after that I took my family to show them that site, and I couldn’t believe what was in front of me there. Nothing had changed, it was like a ghost town right there in the middle of nowhere.”
(LOURENSA): In 2021, Eskom tried to offload the development to the Department of Human Settlements - for affordable housing. But the plan failed.
(LOURENSA): Now, Wilge is up for sale. The asking price hasn't been disclosed.

(LOURENSA): The community of Wilge, meanwhile, continues to live in its shadow.

(LOURENSA): ‘Is there a wish from the community that someone from Eskom will be held accountable for what you have today?’

(ELIJAH MASHIANE): “Of course, of course, justice. We’re all hoping for that. Like maybe someone may come up one day and actually get to tell us the full story of actually what happened.”

(LOURENSA): For Percy, the empty development is a reminder of what was lost.

(LOURENSA): “When you walk past that apartment complex, what does it make you feel like?”
(PERCY MTHSWENI): “I’d say… Angry. Sad at times. Because I, I had very high hopes when that project was still going on. But now it’s all like a dream…”
(LOURENSA): “That’s become a nightmare.”
(PERCY MTSHWENI): “It’s become a nightmare now.”

(FTB)




PROMOS:

PROMO 1:
LOURENSA: “336 apartments built for contractors at the Kusile Power Station. Today they stand completely empty. Where did it all go wrong?”

KEVIN MILEHAM: “It's money that could have been spent building power lines. It's money that could have been spent building hospitals or schools or RDP houses. And it was wasted.”

LOURENSA: We investigate a near billion-rand ghost village - where the money was spent, but the doors never opened.

PROMO 2:
LOURENSA: “A billion rand spent on housing for Kusile workers. But nobody ever moved in.”

DAVID: “When payments become a problem, work can’t continue. It reaches a point where things just stop - and that’s what happened here.”

KEVIN MILEHAM: “Eskom ducks and dives. This I think is a huge embarrassment for them

LOURENSA: How did a mega development built with public funds… go so wrong?

PROMO 3:
LOURENSA: “Three hundred and thirty-six apartments built for contractors at Kusile. and not a single resident in sight. Welcome to Eskom’s very own ghost village.”

PERCY MTSHWENI: “ I had very high hopes when that project was going on. But now, it’s all like a dream…”
LOURENSA: ‘It’s become a nightmare.’
PERCY MTSHWENI: “It’s become a nightmare now.”

TEASER:
LOURENSA: “A billion rand spent on housing for Kusile workers. But nobody ever moved in.”

ELIJAH MASHIANE: ‘Some of the people now today they’re like unemployed, so they’re obviously having some sort of resentment because they lost their jobs, their families aren’t fed.”

(LOURENSA): ‘You sort of planned your future around the development - in studying to become a millwright.’ (ELIJAH MASHIANE): “Yes. You know, I actually had high hopes - employment, you know, everything, you know. And having to see what actually happened to those buildings… what I’ve actually planned for myself now - I have to now, you know, choose a different stream.” (PAUSE) (LOURENSA): While the Wilge Complex stood empty, Eskom had to make a different plan to house the workers. (DAVID SUBTITLES): “What didn’t make sense from a site perspective was that you had this development here. And at the same time people were being accommodated elsewhere. That was difficult to understand.” (LOURENSA): Eskom appointed 46 companies to accommodate contractors in surrounding towns - at a cost of around R1.2 billion. (LOURENSA): One company received the lion’s share of that budget. (LOURENSA): Quatra M Investments, based in eMalahleni, was paid around R894 million. Its role: leasing, managing, and supplying accommodation facilities for Kusile contractors. (LOURENSA): Then we found a connection. (LOURENSA): Abram Masango - Eskom’s former head of capital projects - oversaw Kusile during the years of delays and cost overruns. He’s now under investigation over procurement tied to the project. (LOURENSA): Company records show a link. LOURENSA: So we went to find out more. (LOURENSA): “Hello. Is there anyone we can talk to about the Kusile accommodation contracts?” (EMPLOYEE SUBTITLES): “I spoke to the director, he says he has responded on email.” (LOURENSA): ‘Ya, we did get an email response.’ (EMPLOYEE SUBTITLES): “We did respond on that. There is a court case between ourselves and Eskom unfortunately.” (LOURENSA): “We understand that. But this is a matter of public interest. And we wanted to give you an opportunity to respond on camera.” (EMPLOYEE SUBTITLES): “Unfortunately I can’t phone him again. I’m sure the lawyers will be able to probably provide.” (LOURENSA): Quatra M declined to speak on camera. In writing, one of the directors denied any involvement in Wilge and any improper links to Masango, calling the Wilge project ‘a total disaster that should never have been built.’ (LOURENSA): In court, the two parties are disputing those Kusile contracts and the money tied to them. (LOURENSA): And those who were there say it didn’t happen by accident. (DAVID SUBTITLES): “It was a lot of stuff. It was a lot of politicians I know that came to the site - I’m not gonna say names. It was also in the timeframe that Brian Molefe was running Eskom. I don’t know what went on there - well we all know what went on there - Eskom never paid us.” (FTB) (LOURENSA): To date, not a cent has been recovered. In writing, Eskom confirmed the full project cost of R939 million. (LOURENSA): In 2019, Eskom instituted disciplinary action against the manager responsible. The process concluded in January 2020 with that manager’s dismissal. (LOURENSA): ‘Is this part of the whole corruption cloud hanging over Kusile, and procurement regarding the build of the power station, or should we view this as a separate matter?’ (KEVIN MILEHAM): ‘I think it’s indicative of a much broader systemic problem at Eskom, particularly over the state capture period. But we’re in a situation now where there’s still no accountability, where people still aren’t facing the consequences of their actions.’ (LOURENSA): The independent public integrity and anti-corruption authority, The Special Investigating Unit is probing the project. No criminal charges have been laid. (LOURENSA): For David, Wilge’s failure lies solely with Eskom. (DAVID SUBTITLES): “About two years after that I took my family to show them that site, and I couldn’t believe what was in front of me there. Nothing had changed, it was like a ghost town right there in the middle of nowhere.” (LOURENSA): In 2021, Eskom tried to offload the development to the Department of Human Settlements - for affordable housing. But the plan failed. (LOURENSA): Now, Wilge is up for sale. The asking price hasn't been disclosed. (LOURENSA): The community of Wilge, meanwhile, continues to live in its shadow. (LOURENSA): ‘Is there a wish from the community that someone from Eskom will be held accountable for what you have today?’ (ELIJAH MASHIANE): “Of course, of course, justice. We’re all hoping for that. Like maybe someone may come up one day and actually get to tell us the full story of actually what happened.” (LOURENSA): For Percy, the empty development is a reminder of what was lost. (LOURENSA): “When you walk past that apartment complex, what does it make you feel like?” (PERCY MTHSWENI): “I’d say… Angry. Sad at times. Because I, I had very high hopes when that project was still going on. But now it’s all like a dream…” (LOURENSA): “That’s become a nightmare.” (PERCY MTSHWENI): “It’s become a nightmare now.” (FTB) PROMOS: PROMO 1: LOURENSA: “336 apartments built for contractors at the Kusile Power Station. Today they stand completely empty. Where did it all go wrong?” KEVIN MILEHAM: “It's money that could have been spent building power lines. It's money that could have been spent building hospitals or schools or RDP houses. And it was wasted.” LOURENSA: We investigate a near billion-rand ghost village - where the money was spent, but the doors never opened. PROMO 2: LOURENSA: “A billion rand spent on housing for Kusile workers. But nobody ever moved in.” DAVID: “When payments become a problem, work can’t continue. It reaches a point where things just stop - and that’s what happened here.” KEVIN MILEHAM: “Eskom ducks and dives. This I think is a huge embarrassment for them LOURENSA: How did a mega development built with public funds… go so wrong? PROMO 3: LOURENSA: “Three hundred and thirty-six apartments built for contractors at Kusile. and not a single resident in sight. Welcome to Eskom’s very own ghost village.” PERCY MTSHWENI: “ I had very high hopes when that project was going on. But now, it’s all like a dream…” LOURENSA: ‘It’s become a nightmare.’ PERCY MTSHWENI: “It’s become a nightmare now.” TEASER: LOURENSA: “A billion rand spent on housing for Kusile workers. metadata.Unique Selling Point: A story of how Eskom has wasted hundreds of millions of rand on a "ghost" development, while at the same time seeking to raise power prices for South Africans.
metadata.Summary: More than a decade after it was conceived as a solution for worker accommodation at Eskom’s Kusile Power Station, the Wilge Residential Village remains exactly what it has quietly become: a taxpayer-funded ghost town. Built to house hundreds of construction staff during Kusile’s build, the 336-unit complex has never meaningfully housed anyone. Instead, it has swallowed close to R1-billion, ballooning from an original budget of around R160 million. That works out to roughly R2.5 million per empty apartment. Investigations dating back to the News24 Eskom Files in 2021 exposed how procurement inside the project spiralled into excess, including inflated furniture tenders and alleged collusion between officials and contractors. Items like desks, couches and even leisure equipment were reportedly marked up far beyond market value. The spending kept flowing. Occupants never came. Fast forward to 2025 and now early 2026, and nothing fundamental has changed: • The buildings stand unfinished and unoccupied • The site shows visible decay and vandalism • Attempts to sell or transfer the property have not materialised • Parliament and opposition MPs continue to label it fruitless and wasteful expenditure • The Special Investigating Unit has kept Wilge within broader Eskom corruption probes, but no public recovery of funds or prosecutions linked specifically to the village have been announced. All the while, Eskom has paid for alternative accommodation and transport for workers the village was meant to house, effectively paying twice. The optics are stark. N almost-billion-plus housing estate sitting empty in a province battling housing backlogs and unemployment, while the utility asks consumers for tariff hikes. But Wilge is not just an abandoned development. It is a physical monument to state capture era procurement, weak oversight and consequence-free spending. A concrete reminder that billions were lost not only in coal contracts and power station delays, but also in the small, supposedly practical things. Housing. Beds. Roofs. As of 2026, Wilge is still empty. Still decaying. Still paid for. And there’s still no accountability.
